name: 6U CubeSat bus
description: A shoebox-sized frame with basic wiring. Cheap and quick to build, but it can only carry about 8 kg of equipment.

name: Small satellite bus
description: A washing-machine-sized structure. Carries up to 250 kg of equipment and fuel: enough for a lean lunar orbiter.

name: Medium spacecraft bus
description: A car-sized structure for deep-space missions. Carries up to 1,400 kg including big fuel tanks, but it is heavy and expensive.

name: Large spacecraft bus
description: A flagship-class structure that carries up to 3,000 kg. Only worth it for very ambitious missions: it eats mass, money and time.

name: Body-mounted solar cells
description: Solar cells glued onto the outside of a CubeSat. Light and cheap, but they produce only a few watts.

name: CubeSat deployable panels
description: Small panels that fold out from a CubeSat (0.3 m²). Several times the power of body-mounted cells for about a kilogram.

name: Small deployable solar array
description: Solar panels that unfold after launch (1.5 m²). Far more power than body-mounted cells for a modest mass.

name: Medium deployable solar array
description: 6 m² of solar panels. Enough for a lunar orbiter with several instruments.

name: Large deployable solar array
description: 20 m² of solar panels. Needed far from the Sun: at Mars, sunlight is less than half as strong as at Earth.

name: CubeSat battery (40 Wh)
description: Keeps a CubeSat running while it passes through Earth's shadow, where the solar cells produce nothing.

name: Small battery (400 Wh)
description: Stores energy for the shadowed part of each orbit. Too small a battery forces the spacecraft into safe mode.

name: Medium battery (2,000 Wh)
description: Powers a larger spacecraft through long eclipses, such as low orbits around the Moon.

name: Large battery (6,000 Wh)
description: A big battery bank for power-hungry spacecraft. Heavy, but it protects against eclipses and battery wear.

name: UHF whip antenna
description: A simple radio antenna. Fine for status messages from low Earth orbit, but far too weak to send images from the Moon.

name: S-band patch antenna
description: A flat antenna that sends a few megabits per second from low Earth orbit: good for CubeSat imagery.

name: Medium-gain antenna
description: A focused antenna with a stronger transmitter. The usual choice for sending science data from the Moon.

name: High-gain dish antenna
description: A large dish that must point precisely at Earth. Needed to send meaningful data across the hundreds of millions of kilometres to Mars.

name: Commercial CubeSat computer
description: Cheap off-the-shelf electronics with a 32 Gbit recorder. Radiation can upset it, especially far from Earth.

name: Radiation-tolerant CubeSat computer
description: A small flight computer built to shrug off radiation, with a 64 Gbit recorder. Costs more than commercial boards, but solar storms cannot crash it.

name: Standard flight computer
description: A reliable flight computer with a 256 Gbit data recorder. Good in Earth orbit; vulnerable to deep-space radiation.

name: Radiation-hardened computer
description: Built to survive solar storms and cosmic rays, with a 512 Gbit recorder. Expensive and slower to build, but it protects the whole mission.

name: Magnetorquers
description: Coils that push against Earth's magnetic field to turn the spacecraft. Very cheap, but pointing is rough and they do not work at the Moon or Mars.

name: CubeSat reaction wheels
description: Tiny reaction wheels that point a CubeSat precisely enough for sharp pictures. Better than magnetorquers, but a single failure ends precise pointing.

name: Reaction wheels
description: Spinning wheels that point the spacecraft precisely enough for sharp images. If one fails, pointing suffers.

name: Reaction wheels with a spare
description: Four wheels where three are enough. If one fails, the spare takes over and the mission carries on.

name: Precision pointing system
description: Star trackers plus redundant wheels for very fine pointing. Overkill for most missions.

name: Cold-gas thrusters
description: Puffs of compressed gas. Enough to fight air drag in low Earth orbit, nowhere near enough to reach the Moon.

name: Small hydrazine system
description: A simple rocket engine with 40 kg of fuel. Good for orbit keeping and small manoeuvres.

name: Medium hydrazine system
description: A hydrazine engine with 120 kg of fuel. Enough for a light spacecraft to brake into lunar orbit.

name: Bipropellant engine
description: A powerful engine with 400 kg of fuel: enough to brake into orbit around the Moon or Mars, depending on spacecraft mass.

name: Large bipropellant engine
description: The same engine with 1,000 kg of fuel. More Δv, but every kilogram of fuel also has to be launched.

name: Electric (ion) thruster
description: Five times more efficient than chemical rockets, so 150 kg of xenon goes a long way, but it draws about 600 W of power.

name: CubeSat camera
description: A small visible-light camera. Takes useful pictures from low orbit for very little mass and power.

name: CubeSat multispectral imager
description: Sees in several colours, including infrared, to tell crops, forests, water and cities apart.

name: High-resolution camera
description: A telescope camera that can see objects under a metre across. Produces huge amounts of data and needs precise pointing.

name: Multispectral imager
description: A full-size imager covering many wavelengths for mapping surfaces and minerals.

name: Imaging spectrometer
description: Splits light into hundreds of colours to identify minerals, water ice and gases.

name: Radar sounder
description: Sends radio pulses into the ground to find buried ice layers. Heavy and very power hungry.

name: Magnetometer
description: Measures magnetic fields. Tiny, cheap and produces little data.

name: Radiation monitor
description: Counts energetic particles that threaten astronauts and electronics. Small enough to fit a CubeSat.

name: Laser altimeter
description: Fires laser pulses at the surface and times the echo to map hills and craters to within metres.
